newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's conservatives, Socialists trade charges.
newsitem.headline: Spain's conservatives, Socialists trade charges.

text.p: Spain's ruling conservatives, unleashing their sharpest attack yet on former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, told him on Saturday to face up to his responsibilities for a "dirty war" in the 1980s against Basque rebels and quit as opposition leader.

The political temperature rose further later when the Socialists accused the conservatives of cooking accounts for 1997 to enable Spain to join a single European currency. They announced they would symbolically vote against the government's draft budget.

The exchanges, among the fiercest since Gonzalez stepped down in May after 13 years in power, followed a metaphorical warning by the Socialist chief about the need to eradicate fratricidal forces like those that led to Spain's Civil War.
The Popular Party of his centre-right successor, Jose Maria Aznar, said Gonzalez was no longer fit to head the opposition.

"He must take the political blame for the things that happened during his term as head of the government," Fernando Lopez Amor, the deputy Popular Party spokesman in congress, told Europa Press news agency.
The Supreme Court is considering whether to summon Gonzalez over the 1983-87 campaign of kidnappings, bombings, torture and murder in which 27 people died -- one-third of them by mistake.

Mounting revelations about this campaign waged by the self-styled Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) -- a front for security forces and hired gunmen -- eventually forced Gonzalez to call early elections in March which he lost.

The Socialist leader, who remains a formidable figure in politics, asked his followers this week not to reply to earlier conservative attacks on him against fratricidal strife -- an apparent reference to the 1936-39 Civil War.
"We cannot slide down the slope of demagogy or of the Cain-like politics in which one tries to liquidate one's contenders," Gonzalez told a party rally.
Lopez Amor said the Socialists, still struggling against revelations of past corruption scandals, were incapable of providing a proper opposition and that Gonzalez should have stepped down long ago.
"Their leaders...are incapable not just of recovering the lost ground, but also of providing strategic guidance for a dignified opposition," he said.

Gonzalez has denied any role in the illegal drive against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), a separatist rebel group that has killed nearly 800 people. His first interior minister and other senior officials are on trial for the "dirty war".

The Socialists' blunt charges on Saturday that Aznar and Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato cheated to bring the 1997 draft budget into line with requirements for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) went far beyond the mild criticisms of independent economists who say the figures are optimistic.
"This is the most trick-laden budget ever submitted to parliament," Jose Borrell, the top Socialist in the congressional budget committee, told a news conference.
The tough budget is already certain to go through parliament anyway on the votes of Aznar's Popular Party and those of its Catalan allies.
